newsitem.title: FRANCE: Direct injection engines - wrinkle or revolution?.
newsitem.headline: Direct injection engines - wrinkle or revolution?.

text.p: The diesel's shaky reign as the car's most economical and environmentally friendly engine could soon be over.

Mitsubishi Motors Corp. has introduced a direct injection gasoline engine in Japan that it says can match the diesel for economy while still retaining the traditional gasoline engine's overwhelming superiority in performance produced with smoothness.
Toyota Motor Corp. is launching a similar power plant later this year and all the world's major car makers are said to be working on similar engines.
Direct injection engines have enhanced performance mainly because of technology that can squirt a precise amount of fuel and air straight into the engine's combustion chamber.
Pollution problems are said to be negligible, with no emissions of particulates -- minute, unburned and possibly cancer-causing molecules of fuel -- released by diesel engines.

Diesel-powered cars have become increasingly popular in Europe, especially France, where about 45 percent of new cars are diesels. The surge in sales of these economical, but often rattling and smoky engines, has been partly tax driven, coupled with a huge advantage in fuel economy.
Modern diesels are cleaner and smoother than before, but even their most ardent admirers can't shake the worry over particulates.

"The direct injection engine is almost as efficient as the diesel and, if they can make it reliable, the diesel people would have a big problem," said Professor Douglas Greenhalgh of Britain's Cranfield University.

Mitsubishi, which is launching the new engine in a 1.8-litre, 4-cylinder version of its Galant family car, has an array of claims for the system: 35 percent improvement in fuel economy in city driving; 8 percent better than conventional engines at 75 mph and 40 percent better at idling speeds.

Mitsubishi says the direct injection technology allows a very lean air-to-fuel ratio of 40 to one, compared with the conventional 15 to one, giving 10 percent improvement in power over current engines of the same size.
Mitsubishi's Kiyotaka Takizawa told journalists at the recent Paris Car Show that this engine will become the standard power plant for cars in the 21st century.

"Over a diesel engine of a comparable capacity the new technology Mitsubishi engine yields about 7 percent better fuel economy, 85 percent more power ... zero particulate emissions ... lower noise levels at all speeds, 8 percent lighter in weight and 40 percent lower production costs," Takizawa said.
The direct injection gasoline engine is not a new idea.

About 10 years ago, Volkswagen AG said its engineers had produced one, but it never found its way on to the showroom floor. VW could reproduce all the advantages in efficiency, but was unable to overcome the problem of reliability.
Mitsubishi says that a combination of advances provided by expertise in the Mitubishi group of companies was behind the breakthrough.
Much of it was due to advanced computer-powered engine management, which affords the split second precision to inject just the right combination of air and fuel at the right moment.
But there have been many different power plants over the years that were about to overwhelm the traditional internal combustion engine's faltering dominance.

"If they invented it (the internal combustion engine) today, it's so grossly inefficient, they would have thrown it on the scrapheap straightaway. But they've been improved over the years and there must be over a billion of them around the world today," said Dr. David Wood of Durham University's advanced automobile engineering school in northeast England.
The orbital engine and the rotary engine had their 15 minutes of fame as contenders before fading away. Battery power has been an answer to the need for clean, efficient power for almost 100 years.
The diesel has been refined over the years to give it more power and reform its dirty, noisy image. Some experts say this is still the way to go.

"You brush aside diesel at your peril. The technology is proven, its got a long track record. In Germany every Mercedes taxi driver will show you how mature they are," said Peter Schmidt, analyst at Britain's Automotive Industry Data consultancy.
